objective: By the end of this lesson you can say which IFR takeoff minimums and departure procedures bind a Part 91 pilot, apply the 14 CFR 91.175 tests for going below DA, DH or MDA and for landing, and name the minimum IFR altitude under 91.177 for any point of a flight.
why: Part 91 lets you take off in weather an airline crew may not, so the judgment is yours [[29:24|IPH 1-8]]. On the approach, 91.175 gives three tests that must hold the whole way down, and a missed approach is required the moment one fails [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (e)]]. Below the DA or MDA there is no built-in obstacle protection, and the pilot must see and avoid what is there [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

prereading.what: The whole of 91.175. Read (a) through (j) word for word; the exceptions in (c), (e) and (f) are where pilots go wrong.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.175

prereading.what: 91.177, minimum altitudes for IFR operations: MEA and MOCA, the 1,000 and 2,000 ft rules, and climbs to a higher minimum.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.177

prereading.what: ODPs, SIDs and diverse vector areas: the 200 ft per NM design, takeoff obstacle notes, and who owns obstacle clearance on a Part 91 departure.
prereading.label: AIM 5-2-9

prereading.what: Takeoff minimums, who must use them, the sample takeoff minimums page and the RVR conversion table.
prereading.label: IPH 1-8 to 1-11

prereading.what: Minimum vectoring altitudes, the visual descent point, the visual segment and the vertical descent angle.
prereading.label: AIM 5-4-5e to 5-4-5k

prereading.what: Approach and landing minimums, RVR conversion, circling, and when the missed approach protects you and when it does not.
prereading.label: AIM 5-4-20 and 5-4-21

prereading.label: IPH 4-39 to 4-40

warmup: Think first: You fly your own airplane under Part 91. The departure airport is in fog, 1/4 mile visibility, and the takeoff minimums for your runway are 600-2. At your destination the ATIS reports visibility below the approach minimums. Which of these, if either, does a regulation stop you from doing, and what does the rule actually test at the bottom of the approach?

key_terms.def: The ceiling and visibility for an IFR takeoff. 91.175(f) makes them binding only for Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 operations.
1 SM visibility for airplanes with two engines or less, 1/2 SM for more than two engines, used where no other minimums are published.
A departure, in text or graphic form, built only to keep you clear of obstacles on the climb to the en route structure. It may be flown without a clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or vectors.
Departure end of runway. Departure obstacle protection is measured from here.
Climb in feet per nautical mile. Departures are designed for at least 200 ft per NM unless the procedure asks for more.
Decision altitude (feet MSL) or decision height (feet above the ground): where you decide to continue or start an immediate missed approach.
Minimum descent altitude, feet MSL: the lowest you may descend on final or while circling until you have the required visual references.
The average forward horizontal distance you can see and identify prominent objects from the cockpit in flight. Only the pilot can judge it.
Visual descent point: a point on a nonprecision final from which a stabilized visual descent from the MDA to the runway can begin.
The part of the approach from the DA or MDA to the runway. It has no implied obstacle protection.
Minimum vectoring altitude: the lowest altitude ATC uses for radar vectors in a sector. It can be lower than a charted MEA.
Minimum safe altitude on approach and departure charts: 1,000 ft of obstacle clearance, usually within 25 NM, for emergency use.

chunks.title: Takeoff minimums: who must use them

callout.text: 91.175(f) applies to persons operating under Part 121, 125, 129 or 135. Under it, no IFR takeoff unless the weather is at or above the takeoff minimums prescribed under Part 97. Where none are prescribed: 1 SM visibility for aircraft other than helicopters with two engines or less, 1/2 SM for more than two engines, 1/2 SM for helicopters [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]].

body.p: A Part 91 flight is outside paragraph (f). The IPH says it plainly: Part 91 aircraft are not required to comply with established takeoff minimums, and a zero/zero departure is legal but never advisable. It adds that good judgment would have all instrument pilots follow the minimums the commercial operators must follow [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].

Why it matters: if the departure weather is below the landing minimums for that airport, a failure after takeoff leaves no way back. The choice becomes returning or flying straight to a takeoff alternate, with little time to decide [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].

Nonstandard takeoff minimums are listed by airport in the front of the TPP, and a "T" symbol in the notes of the approach chart tells you they exist [[29:24|IPH 1-8]]. In the IPH sample, Colorado Springs runway 30 reads "600-2 or std. with a min. climb of 220' per NM to 6900" [[29:25|IPH 1-9]]. A ceiling appears in takeoff minimums only when it is needed to see and avoid obstacles in the departure area [[29:24|IPH 1-8]]. When both a ceiling and a visibility are given, both apply [[29:26|IPH 1-10]].

callout.text: Get current visibility right before an IFR departure. The IPH says never launch an IFR flight without it [[29:26|IPH 1-10]].

check.q: You fly a Bonanza under Part 91 from an airport with no published takeoff minimums. Visibility is 1/4 SM. Does 91.175(f) stop you?
check.a: No. Paragraph (f) applies only to Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. The IPH calls such a departure legal but never advisable [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].

chunks.title: Obstacle departure procedures and who keeps you clear

body.p: There are two kinds of departure procedure: ODPs, printed as text or graphics, and SIDs, always graphic. ODPs are recommended for obstacle clearance and may be flown without an ATC clearance unless ATC has assigned a SID or radar vectors. A SID needs a clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]. Part 91 pilots are strongly encouraged to file and fly a DP at night, in marginal VMC and in IMC when one is available [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9c]].

The 91.175(f)(3) rule to use a published ODP sits inside paragraph (f), so it binds the Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 operators [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. For Part 91: if your clearance has no ODP, SID or vectors and an ODP exists, using it is your choice, and you should tell ATC when you use it so they can separate traffic [[29:39|IPH 1-23]]. If you accept a DP in a clearance, you must fly it [[23:296|IFH 10-5]].

callout.text: When you depart IFR under Part 91 and have not filed or been cleared for an ODP, a SID or DVA headings, obstacle clearance is your responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]]. "Radar contact" does not relieve you of terrain and obstruction clearance [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

body.p: The design assumes you cross the DER at least 35 ft above its elevation, reach 400 ft above it before the first turn, and climb at least 200 ft per NM to the minimum IFR altitude. The 40:1 obstacle surface rises at 152 ft per NM out to 25 NM, or 46 NM in mountainous areas. Beyond that, you own obstacle clearance if you are not on a published route, have not reached its MEA or MOCA, or are not at an ATC assigned altitude [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e]]. All of it assumes all engines operating [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e]].

bullets: Low, close-in obstacles: need a steeper climb only within 1 NM, to 200 ft or less above the DER, and bring no higher takeoff minimums [[33:351|AIM 5-2-9e]]. Weather of 300 ft and 1 NM may be needed to see and avoid them [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].
Takeoff minimums obstacles: within 2.6 NM and more than 200 ft above the DER; they bring higher ceiling and visibility minimums [[33:351|AIM 5-2-9e]].
A climb gradient above 200 ft per NM is mandatory when the procedure is part of your clearance, unless higher takeoff minimums are offered and the weather lets you meet them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e]].
VCOA (visual climb over airport): tell ATC before departure and stay within the published visibility distance until the "at or above" altitude [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e]].

callout.text: AIM 5-2-9h before every IFR departure: look at terrain and obstacles, find out if there is an ODP, decide whether you can avoid obstacles visually or should fly it, plan for degraded climb, check for a DVA and its gradient, and read the takeoff obstacle notes for your runway [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h]].

check.q: Your Part 91 clearance is "as filed, climb and maintain 6,000." No SID, no vectors, and the runway has an ODP. Who is responsible for obstacle clearance on the climb?
check.a: You are. Flying the ODP is your choice [[29:39|IPH 1-23]], and without an ODP, SID or DVA in the clearance obstacle clearance rests with the pilot [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

callout.text: 91.175(a): when an instrument approach to a civil airport is necessary, use a standard instrument approach procedure prescribed in Part 97 for that airport, unless otherwise authorized by the FAA. 91.175(b): the authorized DA/DH or MDA is the highest of (1) the one on the procedure, (2) the one prescribed for the pilot in command, and (3) the one for the aircraft equipment available and used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a), (b)]].

body.p: The definitions: a DA is in feet MSL and a DH is in feet above the ground; at either one the pilot decides whether to start an immediate missed approach if the required visual reference is not seen [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]]. An MDA is the lowest altitude, in feet MSL, to which descent is authorized on final or while circling until the pilot sees the required references [[60:10|14 CFR 1.1]].

Each line of minima gives an altitude and a visibility for each aircraft category [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20e]]. Your category comes from VREF, or 1.3 VSO, at maximum certified landing weight [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7a, b]]: A below 91 knots, B 91 to 120, C 121 to 140 [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7e]]. If you must fly faster than your category's range, use the higher category's minimums; a Category A airplane flying a straight-in at 130 knots uses Category C [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7a, b]].

The published number can rise for many reasons: approach category, inoperative equipment in the aircraft or on the ground, and crew qualifications [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Inoperative ground components raise minimums, and an ILS with the glideslope out becomes localizer minimums [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. The Colorado Springs sample shows one such note: Cat D S-LOC 35L visibility increased to RVR 5000 for inoperative ALSF [[29:25|IPH 1-9]].

callout.text: Brief the exact DA or MDA you will use so there is no doubt at the bottom [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Application: say the number and why, for example "LNAV MDA 940, because the box shows LNAV only."

body.p: A civil Part 91 flight at a civil airport that also has military procedures must use the civil one, marked (FAA) at the top of the chart [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5a]]. At a military airport, use the procedures and minimums of the military authority [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(g)]].

check.q: The chart has an LPV DA of 822 ft, but your receiver can only fly LNAV, with an MDA of 940 ft. Which is your authorized minimum?
check.a: 940 ft MDA. The authorized minimum is the highest of the procedure, the PIC and the equipment used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

chunks.title: Going below DA or MDA: the three tests of 91.175(c)

callout.text: No pilot may operate below the authorized MDA, or continue below the authorized DA/DH, unless: (1) the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers; (2) the flight visibility is not less than the visibility prescribed in the approach being used; and (3) at least one listed visual reference for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]].

body.p: The ten visual references in (c)(3) [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]:

bullets: (i) the approach light system, with a limit (below)
(ii) the threshold; (iii) threshold markings; (iv) threshold lights
(v) runway end identifier lights
(vi) the visual glideslope indicator
(vii) the touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings; (viii) touchdown zone lights
(ix) the runway or runway markings; (x) the runway lights

callout.text: With only the approach lights in sight, you may not descend below 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating bars or the red side row bars are also distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

body.p: AIM FIG 2-1-1 shows why the system type matters. The ALSF-2 has red side row bars and the ALSF-1 has red terminating bars; the SSALR, MALSR and MALSF drawings show no red lights at all [[33:122|AIM 2-1-1]]. Application: on a MALSR, the approach lights alone can never take you below 100 ft above TDZE; you need another reference from the list.

Two more limits sit in the same paragraph. The Part 121 and 135 rule adds a touchdown within the touchdown zone, which (c)(1) does not require of other Part 91 flights. Category II and III approaches have visual reference requirements set by the Administrator instead of the list [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. Using an EFVS under 91.176 is a separate path below DA/DH or MDA, with its own equipment and training rules [[29:161|IPH 4-21]].

callout.text: Position, visibility, reference: all three, all the way down. "Continuously" in (c)(1) means the test does not end once you leave the MDA [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]].

check.q: At DA you have the required flight visibility and see the MALSR, nothing else. How far may you descend?
check.a: To 100 ft above TDZE. Below that you need the red terminating or side row bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], which a MALSR does not have [[33:122|AIM 2-1-1]], or another listed reference.

chunks.title: Flight visibility, RVR and the landing rule

callout.text: 91.175(d): for operations other than EFVS operations under 91.176, no pilot may land when the flight visibility is less than the visibility prescribed in the standard instrument approach procedure being used [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]].

body.p: Flight visibility is the average forward horizontal distance from the cockpit in flight at which prominent unlighted objects by day, and lighted objects by night, can be seen and identified [[60:7|14 CFR 1.1]]. ATC gives you reported visibility, but only the pilot can decide whether flight visibility meets the landing minimum. If it is less, go missed whatever the report says [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

Starting the approach is a different question. Part 135 pilots may not begin an instrument approach unless the latest weather report is at or above minimums (with relief once past the FAF), and Part 121 crews may not pass the FAF unless minimums exist [[29:147|IPH 4-7]]. 91.175 has no matching rule for other Part 91 flights; its limits are the (c) and (d) tests [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (d)]]. Interpretation: a Part 91 pilot may begin an approach when the report is below minimums, but may descend below the DA or MDA, and land, only if the flight visibility and references are there. The IPH asks every pilot to review current weather before starting an approach [[29:146|IPH 4-6]].

The table is 91.175(h)(2) [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)]]. When an approach gives an RVR minimum but RVR is not reported for your runway, convert it with this table, except for Category II or III [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]]. For a value between two listed values, use the next higher RVR and do not interpolate: RVR 1800 uses 2400, which is 1/2 mile [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]]. RVR is measured near the touchdown point and shows what a pilot should see looking down the runway; it is horizontal, not slant, range [[29:27|IPH 1-11]].

check.q: The tower reports 1 SM, the chart minimum. At the MDA you see the runway lights, but you judge flight visibility to be about 3/4 SM. May you land?
check.a: No. Landing needs flight visibility not less than prescribed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]], and only the pilot can judge it; go missed regardless of the report [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

chunks.title: The missed approach: when the rule says go

callout.text: 91.175(e): execute an appropriate missed approach immediately (1) when the 91.175(c) requirements are not met while below the MDA, or on arrival at the missed approach point (including a DA/DH) and at any time after that until touchdown; or (2) when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible during a circling maneuver at or above the MDA, unless that is caused only by a normal bank in the circle [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]] [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)]].

body.p: Where the decision falls: on vertically guided approaches the MAP is the DA. Nonprecision and circling procedures share one MAP, found by timing from the FAF, a fix, a NAVAID or a waypoint [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]].

Missed approach obstacle protection assumes you start at the DA/DH, or at the MAP not lower than the MDA, and climb at least 200 ft per NM unless the chart asks for more [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. If you decide early, fly the approach to the MAP at or above the MDA or DH before turning, unless ATC clears otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. Start the missed below the MDA or DA, away from the MAP, or while circling, and following the published missed does not necessarily keep you clear of obstacles or traffic [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].

bullets: Once below the DA or MDA, go missed if the required visibility is lost or the runway environment goes out of sight, except for a normal bank while circling [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].
A rejected landing for any reason (people, equipment or animals on the runway, an unstable approach) is also a missed approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].
Lose visual reference while circling: fly the missed for that approach, with an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]].
Circling: stay at or above the circling altitude until continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate with normal maneuvers [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]].

callout.text: Before starting the approach, decide what you will do in a balked landing beyond the MAP or below the MDA or DA, given the weather and your airplane's performance [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

check.q: Circling at the MDA, you lose sight of the runway for a few seconds only while banked in the turn to base. Must you go missed?
check.a: No. The exception covers loss of sight caused only by a normal bank during the circle [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. If it is anything else, go missed at once.

chunks.title: Risk: the visual segment and the duck-under

callout.text: There is no implied obstacle protection from the MDA or DA to the touchdown point. Obstacles, lighted or not, may penetrate the visual segment surfaces, and it is the pilot's job to see and avoid them during the transition to landing [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

body.p: Designers handle those obstacles by raising the minimums. A penetration of the 34:1 surface keeps the published visibility at 3/4 SM or more. A penetration of the 20:1 surface keeps it at 1 SM or more, with a note banning approaches to that runway at night [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Unlighted penetrations can bring the note "Procedure NA at Night", and a penetration may also mean no VDP is published [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. On RNAV charts, a gray shaded line from the MDA to the runway shows the visual segment is clear on the 34:1 slope; no gray means it is not [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

bullets: Do not descend below the MDA before the VDP. Between the VDP and the MAP a descent may be inadvisable or impossible. Without the equipment to identify the VDP, fly as if none were published [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].
VDPs apply to LP and LNAV minima, not to LPV or LNAV/VNAV [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m]].

A published VDA is advisory and gives no obstacle protection below the MDA. "Visual Segment- Obstacles" in the profile means the VDA was removed because following it would meet obstacles [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5k]] [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k]].

body.p: The trap has a name. AC 60-22 calls it the duck-under syndrome: sneaking a peek by descending below minimums, from a belief in a built-in fudge factor or an unwillingness to admit defeat and fly the missed [[9:15|AC 60-22 4d]]. The PHAK lists the same pitfall and notes it can happen en route too, as a descent below the minimum en route altitude [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

The IPH warns that any delay in deciding at the DA, DH, MDA or MAP risks hitting obstacles that penetrate the visual surface [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. Shallow fog can let you see the runway from above and lose it in the flare, so be ready to go around. Single-pilot crews have it harder, since one pilot must keep flying the instruments while looking for the runway [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

check.q: You reach the MDA a mile before the VDP and see the runway. Your GPS shows an advisory glidepath to the runway. Why not follow it down now?
check.a: Descent below the MDA should not start before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]], and an advisory vertical path gives no obstacle protection below the MDA [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k]].

callout.text: 91.177(a): except when necessary for takeoff or landing, or unless otherwise authorized by the FAA, no IFR flight below (1) the minimum altitudes in Parts 95 and 97, or (2) where none are prescribed, 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course over a designated mountainous area, and 1,000 ft above it in any other case [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

body.p: MOCA: where both an MEA and a MOCA are published, you may fly below the MEA down to the MOCA if the navigation signals you need are available. If you are navigating by VOR, only within 22 NM of that VOR, by your reasonable estimate [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. Part 95 says the MOCA assures obstacle clearance and VOR reception within 22 NM of the station, and that an off-airway MEA covers 4 NM each side of the course unless otherwise stated [[60:712|14 CFR 95.1]].

callout.text: 91.177(b): a climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude begins immediately after passing the point where it applies. Where ground obstructions intervene, cross that point at or above the MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]].

body.p: The designated mountainous areas are listed in Part 95, Subpart B, starting with the Eastern United States area in 95.13 [[60:713|14 CFR 95.13]].
These rules apply to every IFR flight, in IFR or VFR weather, with an assigned altitude or a VFR-on-top clearance [[29:95|IPH 2-35]].

callout.text: Off the charts: 1,000 ft, or 2,000 in the mountains, above anything within 4 NM [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

check.q: You fly an off-airway direct route with no published minimum altitude, outside any mountainous area. The highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course is 2,349 ft MSL. What is your lowest legal IFR altitude?
check.a: 3,349 ft MSL: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

chunks.title: Altitudes ATC and the charts give you

body.p: MVA: ATC builds these sectors for radar vectoring. Each gives 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle, 2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas (sometimes 1,000 ft there with ATC surveillance), and at least 300 ft above the floor of controlled airspace. Some MVAs are lower than the MEA or MOCA nearby, and ATC assigns IFR altitudes at or above the MVA while vectoring [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5e]].

OROCA gives 1,000 ft of clearance (2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas) but is not checked for navigation signal, radar or radio coverage. It is for situational awareness, planning and in-flight contingencies [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5e]]. The MSA on approach and departure charts is for emergency use: 1,000 ft above all obstacles, normally within 25 NM, but it does not assure navigation signal coverage [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5c]].

callout.text: 91.175(i): on an unpublished route or radar vectors, when you get an approach clearance, also comply with 91.177 and maintain the last assigned altitude until established on a segment of a published route or approach, unless ATC assigns another altitude. Once established, published altitudes apply to each following segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].

body.p: You are not established while below the published approach altitudes [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7f]], and a procedure turn does not count as a segment until you reach the fix it is based on [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7f]]. With radar vectors to final, a timed approach from a holding fix, or a "No PT" procedure, no procedure turn unless ATC clears you for one [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]].

Stepdown fix altitudes inside the final segment apply when you fly to an MDA line. They do not apply on lines with a DA, where the vertical guidance gives the clearance. Outside the final segment you must respect them on every kind of approach [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b]].

check.q: Approach says: "Turn left heading 200, maintain 3,000 until established on the final approach course, cleared RNAV runway 23 approach." You intercept the final course. When may you descend?
check.a: Only once established on a published segment; then the published altitudes for that segment apply [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. You are not established while below the published approach altitudes [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7f]].

chunks.title: Fly it: continue or go missed at each point

head: Where you are
What the rule asks
Action
rows: Vectored, cleared for the approach
Last assigned altitude until established [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]
Hold the altitude; descend only on a published segment
Final segment to an MDA
Stepdown altitudes apply on MDA lines [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b]]
Descend fix by fix, never below a stepdown altitude
At the MDA, before the VDP
Do not descend below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]
Level at the MDA, look for references
At the VDP or DA, references and flight visibility met
Continue at a normal descent rate
Approach lights only
Not below 100 ft above TDZE without red bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]
Stop at 100 ft above TDZE unless another reference appears
At the MAP or DA, tests not met
Missed approach immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]
Go missed, fly the published missed
Below the MDA, a test fails
Missed approach immediately [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]
Go missed; the published missed may not give obstacle clearance from here [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]
Over the threshold
No landing if flight visibility is less than prescribed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]]
Land, or go around

body.p: Apply it to the Fort Campbell sample in f4. With LNAV only, the MDA is 940 ft and its height above touchdown is 368 ft; the VDP is 1.0 NM from RW23 and applies to LNAV only [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. Application: at 940 ft you level off, hold it to the VDP, and descend only with the references, the flight visibility and a normal descent available. If none of that is true at RW23, you go missed.

check.q: At the MAP of a nonprecision approach you see the runway lights, flight visibility is fine, but you are too high and fast to reach the runway with a normal descent. What now?
check.a: Go missed. (c)(1) requires a continuous position for a normal descent with normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]], and failing it at the MAP requires an immediate missed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]].

bullets: Treating "legal for Part 91" as "safe." Fix: if you could not return and land, you need a plan, and the IPH advises following takeoff minimums anyway [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].
Thinking ATC or radar contact keeps you clear of obstacles on an unassigned departure. Fix: under Part 91 without an ODP, SID or DVA in the clearance, it is your job [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].
Accepting a SID or ODP with a gradient you cannot make. Fix: it is mandatory once in the clearance, unless you can use higher takeoff minimums [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e]].
Using the chart DA when the equipment flies only a higher line. Fix: the highest of procedure, PIC and equipment [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].
Going below 100 ft above TDZE on approach lights alone. Fix: red terminating or side row bars, or another reference [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].
Landing because the report said minimums. Fix: flight visibility is the test, and you judge it [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].
Descending below the MDA before the VDP, or on an advisory glidepath. Fix: hold the MDA to the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]; see and avoid obstacles below it [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k]].
Descending as soon as the vector crosses the final course. Fix: last assigned altitude until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]].
Using a MOCA beyond 22 NM of the VOR you navigate by. Fix: within 22 NM only [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

check.q: Which single word in 91.175(c)(1) catches pilots who see the runway at the MDA and then get low and slow on the way in?
check.a: "Continuously": the aircraft must stay in a position for a normal descent with normal maneuvers the whole way, or the missed is required [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (e)]].

scenario.title: A low IFR day trip in your own airplane
scenario.setup: You fly your single-engine airplane under Part 91, Category A, with a GPS that can fly LPV. The departure airport has nonstandard takeoff minimums for your runway: "600-2 or std. with a min. climb of 220' per NM to 6900," and a textual ODP. The weather is 500 overcast, 1 SM. Your route includes a direct off-airway leg over a designated mountainous area with no published minimum altitude. At the destination you will fly an RNAV (GPS) approach with LPV and LNAV lines; fog is forecast to form near arrival time.

questions.q: Is the departure legal, and what does the IPH advise?
questions.a: Legal: takeoff minimums in 91.175(f) bind only Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. The IPH says good judgment calls for following them anyway [[29:24|IPH 1-8]]. The weather is below 600-2, so the protected way out is the other option: standard minimums with at least 220 ft per NM to 6,900 [[29:25|IPH 1-9]].

questions.q: At 100 knots groundspeed you climb 600 fpm. Do you meet 220 ft per NM, and who keeps you clear of obstacles if the clearance is just "as filed"?
questions.a: 600 x 60 / 100 = 360 ft per NM, more than 220. Without an ODP, SID or DVA in the clearance, obstacle clearance is yours [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]]; flying the ODP is your choice, and you should tell ATC you are using it [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

questions.q: On the off-airway leg the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course is 9,840 ft MSL. What is your minimum IFR altitude?
questions.a: 11,840 ft MSL: 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM in a designated mountainous area [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

questions.q: Approach vectors you and says "maintain 4,000 until established, cleared RNAV approach." Then your receiver drops from LPV to LNAV. What changes?
questions.a: Keep 4,000 until established on a published segment [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. Your authorized minimum becomes the LNAV MDA, since it is the one for the equipment you are using [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]], and the VDP now applies to you [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m]].

questions.q: The ATIS now reports visibility below the LNAV minimum. May you start the approach?
questions.a: Interpretation: 91.175 has no rule against starting it; the limits are flight visibility and references at the MDA and for landing [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (d)]]. Part 135 and 121 do have such rules [[29:147|IPH 4-7]]. Only you can judge flight visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

questions.q: At the MDA, past the VDP, you see only the MALSR, with good flight visibility. At 100 ft above TDZE nothing else is in sight. What do you do, and what is the trap?
questions.a: Go missed: approach lights alone allow no lower than 100 ft above TDZE without red bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], and the missed is required as soon as a test fails [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. From below the MDA the published missed may not clear obstacles [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. The trap is the duck-under: pressing on for a peek [[9:15|AC 60-22 4d]].

skills.do: Given an approach chart, your equipment and the weather at each point (vectors, FAF, MDA or DA, VDP, MAP, below minimums, circling, landing), say whether you may continue or must go missed, and name the 91.175 paragraph that decides it.
skills.practice: Take three approaches you fly often: one with an LPV line, one LNAV, one with circling. For each, write the authorized minimum for your equipment [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]], the lowest altitude with approach lights only [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]] and where the VDP and MAP are [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]] [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f]]. Then have a safety pilot or instructor call out what you "see" at each point in the simulator and say continue or missed aloud.

quiz.q: Under 91.175(f), what takeoff visibility applies to a Part 135 operator in a single-engine airplane where Part 97 prescribes no takeoff minimums?
options: 1/2 SM
1 SM
300 ft and 1 SM
No minimum
quiz.why: Where none are prescribed, aircraft other than helicopters with two engines or less use 1 SM [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]].

quiz.q: When may an ODP be flown without an ATC clearance?
options: Never; every departure procedure needs a clearance
Only at a towered airport
Unless ATC has assigned a SID or radar vectors
Only in VMC
quiz.why: ODPs may be flown without ATC clearance unless an alternate departure procedure, a SID or radar vector, has been specifically assigned [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

quiz.q: Which takeoff obstacles call for a steeper climb but do NOT bring higher takeoff minimums?
options: Low, close-in obstacles
Takeoff minimums obstacles
Obstacles beyond 25 NM
Obstacles that set the MVA
quiz.why: Low, close-in obstacles need a higher gradient only within 1 NM, to 200 ft or less above the DER, and do not require increased takeoff minimums [[33:351|AIM 5-2-9e]].

quiz.q: The chart DA is 1,250 ft, the minimum prescribed for you as PIC is 1,350 ft, and your equipment allows the chart DA. What is the authorized DA?
options: The lower of the two
quiz.why: The authorized DA/DH or MDA is the highest of the procedure's, the PIC's and the equipment's [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

quiz.q: How does a DH differ from a DA?
options: A DH is a height above the ground; a DA is an altitude above mean sea level
A DH is for circling; a DA is for straight-in
There is no difference
A DH is used only for VFR approaches
quiz.why: DA is expressed in feet MSL, DH in feet AGL [[60:5|14 CFR 1.1]].

quiz.q: With only the approach light system in sight, and no red terminating or side row bars, how low may you go?
options: To the DA only
To touchdown
To 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation
To 200 ft above the airport elevation
quiz.why: Not below 100 ft above TDZE using the approach lights unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also distinctly visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

quiz.q: Who decides whether the flight visibility meets the landing minimum?
options: The tower controller
The pilot
The ASOS
The approach controller
quiz.why: Only the pilot can determine whether flight visibility meets the landing requirement [[23:313|IFH 10-22]].

quiz.q: An approach requires RVR 5000, but RVR is not reported for that runway. What visibility do you need?
options: 3/4 SM
1/2 SM
1 SM
quiz.why: Under the 91.175(h) table, RVR 5000 equals 1 statute mile [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)]].

quiz.q: Where no minimum IFR altitude is prescribed and you are outside a mountainous area, 91.177 requires at least:
options: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 2 NM
2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM
1,000 ft above the terrain directly below
quiz.why: In any case other than a designated mountainous area: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Under Part 91 you plan to depart in fog with 1/8 SM visibility from a runway with no published takeoff minimums. What do the sources say?
options: Illegal: 1 SM standard minimums apply to all IFR takeoffs
Legal only with ATC approval
Legal, but the IPH calls a zero/zero departure never advisable
Legal only for multiengine airplanes
final_quiz.why: 91.175(f) binds Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. The IPH says Part 91 need not comply, a zero/zero departure is legal but never advisable [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].

final_quiz.q: Takeoff minimums read "600-2 or std. with a min. climb of 220' per NM to 6900." The weather is 400 overcast, 1 SM, and today your airplane can make only 180 ft per NM. The ODP is in your clearance. What applies?
options: You can depart; Part 91 never needs the gradient
You meet neither option: the gradient is mandatory in the clearance and the weather is below 600-2
You may substitute standard minimums with 180 ft per NM
Climb gradients apply only to SIDs
final_quiz.why: A published gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of the clearance, unless higher takeoff minimums are offered and the weather allows them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e]]. Here neither works, so ask for something else or wait.

final_quiz.q: You fly an ODP and ATC then vectors you off it with an altitude lower than the one on the ODP. What happens to the ODP?
options: It stays in force; climb back to it
It is canceled, and ATC assumes terrain and obstacle clearance
You must fly both at once
It changes into a SID
final_quiz.why: Aircraft may be vectored off an ODP or issued a lower altitude, at which time the ODP is canceled and ATC assumes responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h]].

final_quiz.q: The destination reports visibility below the LNAV minimum. You are Part 91. May you begin the approach?
options: No; 91.175 bans starting it
Only if past the FAF when the report comes
Only with a Part 135 waiver
Yes, interpretation: 91.175 has no such ban for Part 91; the tests are flight visibility and references below the MDA and for landing
final_quiz.why: The begin-the-approach rules are in Part 135 and Part 121 [[29:147|IPH 4-7]]. 91.175 tests flight visibility and references for going below the MDA and for landing [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (d)]].

final_quiz.q: Your descent from the MDA would touch down past the touchdown zone, but at a normal rate with normal maneuvers. You fly Part 91, not 121 or 135. Does 91.175(c)(1) forbid it?
options: Yes, every operation must touch down in the TDZ
No; the touchdown zone clause applies to Part 121 and 135 operations
Yes, unless the runway is longer than 5,000 ft
Only at night
final_quiz.why: The touchdown zone language in (c)(1) is limited to operations under Part 121 or 135 [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]. Runway length is still your problem.

final_quiz.q: Following an advisory GPS glidepath below the MDA on a chart that says "Visual Segment- Obstacles" in the profile. What is the risk?
options: None; the advisory path is protected
Only a loss of GPS signal
The VDA was removed because following it below the MDA can meet obstacles; you must see and avoid them
ATC will cancel your approach clearance
final_quiz.why: That note replaces the VDA when an obstacle would require deviating from it; pilots following a descent angle below the MDA there may meet obstacles and must visually avoid them [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k]].

final_quiz.q: You are vectored to final and cleared for the approach. The chart shows a procedure turn. May you fly it?
options: Yes, it is always part of the approach
Only if the wind requires it
Only in a nonradar environment
No, not unless ATC clears you for it
final_quiz.why: With a radar vector to the final approach course or fix, no pilot may make a procedure turn unless cleared to do so by ATC [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]].

final_quiz.q: ATC vectors you at 2,500 ft in an area where the airway MEA is 3,000 ft. Is that consistent with the AIM?
options: Yes; MVAs can be lower than nonradar MEAs, and vectoring altitudes are at or above the MVA
No; ATC must never assign below an MEA
Only in Class G airspace
Only for VFR aircraft
final_quiz.why: Some MVAs may be lower than nonradar MEAs or MOCAs, and IFR altitude assignments while vectoring are at or above the MVA [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5e]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC near the destination your navigator fails and you are unsure of your position. What does the MSA on the approach chart give you?
options: Guaranteed navigation and radar coverage
1,000 ft above all obstacles within its radius, normally 25 NM, without assured signal coverage
2,000 ft clearance everywhere
An altitude ATC must assign you
final_quiz.why: MSAs are for emergency use and provide 1,000 ft of clearance over all obstacles, normally within 25 NM, but do not necessarily assure navigation signal coverage [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5c]].

final_quiz.q: You hold a VFR-on-top clearance over mountains, in clear air above a cloud deck. May you fly below the MEA?
options: Yes, you are VFR
Yes, if you stay 1,000 ft above the clouds
No; IFR minimum altitude rules still apply on VFR-on-top
Only below 18,000 ft
final_quiz.why: On an IFR flight plan cleared to VFR conditions on top, pilots may not fly below minimum en route IFR altitudes [[29:95|IPH 2-35]] [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

final_quiz.q: At the MDA the circling area is in sight, and a cloud hides the whole airport as you turn downwind, wings at a normal bank. What does 91.175(e) require?
options: Continue; you are at the MDA
An immediate missed approach; the loss is not caused only by the bank
Descend to get below the cloud
Ask ATC for permission to continue
final_quiz.why: A missed approach is required when an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible while circling at or above the MDA, unless caused only by a normal bank [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. Turn first toward the landing runway to join the missed [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]].

final_quiz.q: You start the missed 1.5 NM before the MAP of a nonprecision approach. The missed begins with a right turn. Unless ATC says otherwise, what should you do?
options: Fly the approach to the MAP at or above the MDA before turning
Turn right at once to save time
Climb straight ahead for 5 minutes
Turn toward the MSA sector with the lowest altitude
final_quiz.why: When an early missed is executed, fly the IAP to the MAP at or above the MDA or DH before any turn, unless ATC clears otherwise; no allowance is made for an early turn [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

final_quiz.q: You fly into a military airport on an IFR flight plan. Whose approach and takeoff minimums apply?
options: The civil standard minimums of 91.175(f)
Whatever the pilot chooses
Those prescribed by the military authority having jurisdiction
None; military fields have no minimums for civil aircraft
final_quiz.why: Civil aircraft into or out of a military airport comply with the procedures and minimums of the military authority [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(g)]], and normally need prior permission [[33:397|AIM 5-4-5a]].

takeaways: Takeoff minimums and the ODP rule in 91.175(f) bind 121, 125, 129 and 135; Part 91 is legal below them, but rarely wise.
Not cleared for an ODP, SID or DVA? Obstacle clearance on the climb is yours, radar contact or not.
Your minimum is the highest of the chart, the PIC and the equipment.
Below DA or MDA: normal descent position, flight visibility and one listed reference, continuously.
Approach lights alone stop you at 100 ft above TDZE without red bars.
You judge flight visibility; land only if it meets the chart, whatever the report.
91.177: published minimums, or 1,000 ft (2,000 in the mountains) above anything within 4 NM; on vectors, keep the last assigned altitude until established.
cfi_notes: IFH 10-21 lists the visual references with the approach light system as a plain item and "visual approach slope indicator (VASI)" [[23:312|IFH 10-21]]. The CFR adds the 100 ft above TDZE limit for approach lights and says "visual glideslope indicator" [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]. Teach the CFR list.

IPH 2-35 says pilots may go down to the MOCA "only when within 22 NM of the VOR" [[29:95|IPH 2-35]]. 91.177(a)(1) limits the 22 NM condition to aircraft using VOR for navigation, with the navigation signals available [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. Teach the CFR wording.
IFH 10-5 points to "paragraph 5-2-7 of the AIM" for departure procedures [[23:296|IFH 10-5]]; the current AIM covers them in 5-2-9 [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

The sources disagree on where ODPs are in the TPP. AIM 5-2-9g says Section L, then in the next item says the T symbol refers users to Section C [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]] [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9g]]. IFH 10-5 says section C [[23:296|IFH 10-5]]. Have pilots find the takeoff minimums page in their own current TPP or app.

The source note under 91.175 lists amendments through Amdt. 91-345B [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175]], but the sources do not show what each one changed. Teach (f) as printed now: its first sentence limits the whole paragraph to Parts 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]].

Interpretation flag: the claim that Part 91 may begin an approach with weather reported below minimums rests on 91.175 having no such rule, plus the IPH description of the Part 135 and 121 rules [[29:147|IPH 4-7]]. Present it as interpretation and pair it with the IPH advice to review current weather first [[29:146|IPH 4-6]].
The Fort Campbell and Colorado Springs charts are IPH samples from 2010 marked not for navigation [[29:180|IPH 4-40]] [[29:25|IPH 1-9]]. Use them for reading practice only.

The PHAK duck-under line reads "a pilot may want to admit that the landing cannot be completed" [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]], which seems to have lost a "not". AC 60-22 states the intended idea: an unwillingness to admit defeat and shoot the missed [[9:15|AC 60-22 4d]].

AC 61-98E lists takeoff and landing under IFR (91.175) and minimum safe altitudes (91.119 and 91.177) in its Part 91 review guide for flight reviews [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]] [[15:47|AC 61-98E App E]]. Instrument pilots: run the decide game and the fly-it table aloud.
gaps: Your airplane's climb performance at the day's weight and temperature, needed to check a climb gradient, comes from the POH or AFM, not these sources.
EFVS operations under 91.176 and the 61.66 training they need are only mentioned; the full rules are outside this lesson.
Category II and III visual reference and equipment requirements are set by the Administrator and are not taught here.
The current Inoperative Components table and TPP legend are not in the sources (the IFH shows a 2010 sample); use your current TPP or chart provider.
The TERPS criteria behind the 40:1, 34:1 and 20:1 surfaces (FAA Order 8260.3) are not in the sources beyond the summaries quoted.

activities.title: True or false: departing IFR under Part 91
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A Part 91 pilot must meet published takeoff minimums.
A SID may be flown only after ATC clears you for it.
cards.why: True. ATC clearance must be received before flying a SID [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

cards.s: If you accept a departure procedure in your clearance, you must comply with it.
Departure obstacle protection assumes the first turn at 400 ft above the DER elevation, unless the procedure says higher.
cards.why: True. Climb to 400 ft above the DER elevation before the initial turn [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e]].

cards.s: Once departure says "radar contact," ATC owns terrain clearance on any IFR departure.
cards.why: False. Radar contact does not relieve the pilot of terrain and obstruction clearance [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

cards.s: Departure procedures assume all engines operating.
cards.why: True. Engine-failure contingency planning is the operator's job [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e]].

activities.title: Read the Fort Campbell minimums
activities.intro: Drag each label to its pin on the sample chart.

pins.label: Category B circling height above airport

activities.why: HOOAH carries the FAF symbol; the V with "1.0 NM to RW23" is the VDP, marked for LNAV only; the small numbers after each DA or MDA give the height above touchdown or, for circling, above the airport (elevation 572) [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. 822 - 572 = 250, 940 - 572 = 368 and 1,040 - 572 = 468.

activities.title: Does it count as a visual reference?
activities.intro: Tap each thing you see at the DA or MDA, then tap where it belongs under 91.175(c)(3).
buckets: Counts only to 100 ft above TDZE

items.t: ALSF-1 approach lights without the red terminating bars yet
Taxiway edge lights beside the runway

activities.why: The ten references are approach lights (with the 100 ft limit), threshold, threshold markings and lights, REIL, visual glideslope indicator, touchdown zone and its markings and lights, the runway, its markings and lights [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]. Taxiway lights, the beacon and towers are not on the list.

activities.title: From vectors to touchdown
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps of an LNAV approach in order, then tap Check.
steps: Cleared for the approach on a vector: keep the last assigned altitude
Established on a published segment: descend to that segment's altitude
Cross the FAF and step down to the MDA
Hold the MDA until the VDP
With references, flight visibility and a normal descent, leave the MDA
Land only if flight visibility is not less than the chart minimum
activities.why: Last assigned altitude until established, then published altitudes [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]; stepdowns on MDA lines [[33:401|AIM 5-4-5b]]; no descent below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]; the three tests [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]; landing visibility [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)]].

activities.title: Which paragraph says it?
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then what it says.

pairs.r: Use a Part 97 standard approach at a civil airport
Authorized minimum is the highest of procedure, PIC and equipment
Three tests before going below DA or MDA
No landing below the prescribed flight visibility
When an immediate missed approach is required
1,000 or 2,000 ft above obstacles within 4 NM

activities.title: Work the minimums
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane climbs 500 fpm at 90 knots groundspeed. How many feet per NM is that? (1 decimal)
items.why: 500 x 60 / 90 = 333.3 ft per NM, enough for the 220 ft per NM in the IPH sample [[29:25|IPH 1-9]].

items.q: Fort Campbell sample: LPV DA 822 ft. Suppose a high-minimums rule, like the one the IPH describes for some Part 121, 125 and 135 PICs, adds 100 ft to your DA. Your equipment can fly LPV. What is your authorized DA?
items.why: 822 + 100 = 922 [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. The highest of procedure, PIC and equipment governs [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

items.q: TDZE is 572 ft. You see only the approach lights, no red bars. What is the lowest MSL altitude you may descend to?
Off-airway in a designated mountainous area, no published minimum. The highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course is 6,870 ft MSL. Minimum IFR altitude?
The chart minimum is RVR 2000, and RVR is not reported. What visibility in statute miles do you need? (decimal)
items.why: Between listed values use the next higher RVR, 2400, which is 1/2 SM; do not interpolate [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20a]] [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)]].

activities.title: Fog at the localizer: decide at each step
activities.intro: You fly a Category A airplane under Part 91 to a LOC runway 9 approach with a MALSF, an MDA and a VDP. The chart visibility is 1 SM. Fog is building.

steps.s: The ATIS reports 3/4 SM. Do you start the approach?
options: No, it is illegal under 91.175 to start it
Yes, interpretation: no Part 91 rule bans it; you will decide at the MDA on flight visibility and references
Only after asking for a waiver
Only if you file as Part 135
steps.why: The start-of-approach bans are Part 135 and 121 rules [[29:147|IPH 4-7]]; 91.175 tests what you see at and below the MDA [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)]].

steps.s: Approach clears you: "Maintain 2,500 until established on the localizer, cleared LOC runway 9." The needle centers. Now?
options: Descend to the MDA at once
Descend to the published altitude for the segment you are now on
Hold 2,500 to the MAP
Fly the procedure turn
steps.why: Once established on a published segment, its published altitudes apply [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(i)]]. No procedure turn on vectors unless cleared [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(j)]].

steps.s: Level at the MDA, 2 NM before the VDP, you see the MALSF through the haze. What do you do?
options: Descend now toward the lights
Stay at the MDA until the VDP
Go missed
Turn toward the lights to line up
steps.why: Do not descend below the MDA before the VDP [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]].

steps.s: At the VDP the MALSF is still all you see, and flight visibility looks like 1 SM. How low may you go?
options: To touchdown
To 100 ft above TDZE, unless another listed reference appears
Nowhere: approach lights do not count
To 50 ft above TDZE
steps.why: Approach lights alone take you no lower than 100 ft above TDZE without red bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], and the MALSF has none [[33:122|AIM 2-1-1]].

steps.s: At 150 ft above TDZE the approach lights fade into fog and nothing else is visible. What now?
options: Hold altitude and wait for the runway
Descend a little to get under the fog
Go missed immediately, knowing the published missed may not clear obstacles from this low
Ask the tower for the RVR
steps.why: When a (c) requirement fails below the MDA, the missed is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. From below the MDA, the published missed does not assure obstacle clearance [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]]. Pressing on is the duck-under [[9:15|AC 60-22 4d]].
